transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I guess... it's a lot of things, really, but what finally pushed me to actually pick up the phone and come in today is that my eating has just been completely all over the place. And I mean, really all over the place. It’s like I can’t find any sort of normal routine or middle ground anymore. 

Some weeks, I’ll make a whole meal and I just sit there and I barely touch my dinner. I'll just push the food around my plate and I have absolutely zero appetite, like the thought of chewing and swallowing is just too much effort, or I'm just completely disconnected from the idea of food. But then, it completely flips. Other nights—and this is what's really been bothering me—I’ll wait until the house is totally quiet, you know, after everyone’s finally gone to bed and the TV is off, and I’ll just wander in there. I'll stand right there in the middle of the kitchen, sometimes not even turning the overhead lights on, just standing by the counter eating crackers and sweets. I'll go through a whole sleeve of saltines or whatever cookies or chocolate I can find hiding in the back of the pantry, just standing there in the quiet by myself. It’s just so extreme, going from practically fasting at the dinner table in front of everybody to standing alone in the dark eating junk food, and I just... I don't know, it just really started to worry me that I can't seem to regulate it at all.
Aside from the changes in your eating, have you noticed a low or depressed mood, or a loss of interest and pleasure in things you used to enjoy, most of the day nearly every day?

Well, yes, actually. That's... that's a big part of it, I think. It’s not just the food. I go through these stretches—and they can last for weeks, it feels like—where everything in the house just feels so... gray. And heavy. It’s hard to even explain because it’s not like I’m crying all the time, it’s more like this weight settles over everything. 

I’ll just sit there at the kitchen table, maybe with a cup of coffee that’s gone completely cold because I forgot to drink it, and I just feel so incredibly empty. And the strange thing is, I’ll sit there trying to figure out why, running through the day in my head, but nothing terrible has happened. Nobody called with bad news, the bills are paid, the weather might even be perfectly nice outside, but inside, it’s just this hollow, dragging feeling. I used to love tending to my houseplants—I have a whole sunroom full of them, pothos and ferns and these beautiful orchids that took me years to figure out how to care for—but lately, during these stretches, I’ll look at them and just feel nothing. I know they need watering, I know the leaves need dusting, but I just can't bring myself to care. The joy is just completely siphoned out of it. And it’s like that most of the day, day after day, until I just feel like I'm moving through molasses. It makes getting out of bed feel like a monumental task, let alone doing anything I used to find fun.
During those nighttime episodes when you're eating crackers and sweets, do you feel like you can't stop or control how much you're eating once you start?

Well, no, not exactly. It's not like I feel... out of control, or like I'm completely possessed and can't stop my hands from moving. It’s not a frantic thing, if that makes sense. It’s more like... I just don't care to stop? Or I'm just so numb that the eating is the only thing happening. 

I'll be standing there in the kitchen, right by the island where the moonlight comes through the blinds—because I really don't like turning the lights on, it feels too harsh, you know, when the whole house is asleep and it's just me and the refrigerator hum. And I'll open a sleeve of saltines. And I'll eat one, and it's dry, and it doesn't even taste particularly good, but I'll just keep eating them, one after another. It's almost methodical. I'm fully aware that I'm doing it, and I know I could just fold the plastic wrapper over and put the box back in the pantry and walk upstairs to bed. I know I have the physical ability to stop. But I just... don't. I'll just stand there, shifting my weight from one foot to the other on the linoleum, chewing and swallowing, chewing and swallowing, until the sleeve is empty or until I just finally feel tired enough to go back upstairs. So it's not that I can't control it, it's just that the control doesn't seem to matter in that moment. It's more of a quiet surrender to the quietness of the house, I suppose.

Do these episodes of skipping meals and then eating crackers and sweets at night happen only during the weeks when you're feeling low and empty, or do they also occur during times when your mood feels normal?

Well, that’s... that’s a really interesting question, actually. I’ve had to think about that myself, because you’d think it would just be when I’m feeling that awful, heavy emptiness, right? That would make sense. You’d think the low mood and the weird eating would just go hand-in-hand, like a package deal. But... no. No, it’s not just then. 

Even when I’m feeling perfectly fine—when the fog has lifted and I’m actually getting out of bed without it feeling like I’m dragging a boulder behind me, and I’m back to watering my orchids and actually enjoying the sunshine coming through the sunroom windows—I still do it. It’s so strange. I’ll have had a perfectly normal day, maybe even a good day, where I felt light and capable, and then dinner rolls around and I’m just... not interested. I’ll sit at the table and push the food around, just like when I’m depressed. And then, sure enough, 11:30 or midnight hits, the house is completely silent, and there I am again. Standing in the dark kitchen in my slippers, opening a box of crackers or hunting down whatever chocolate is left in the pantry. 

It’s almost like it’s become its own separate thing, completely untethered from how I’m actually feeling emotionally. I used to try to analyze it, standing there chewing on a saltine, thinking, "Am I sad right now? Is that why I'm doing this?" But I’m not. Sometimes I’m just standing there, feeling totally fine, maybe even thinking about a book I’m reading or what I need to do the next day, but I’m still just... eating in the dark. It’s really baffling to me, to be honest. It just doesn’t seem to care whether I’m in one of those dark, empty stretches or if I’m having a perfectly decent, normal week. It just happens regardless.

Have you had episodes like this low, empty mood before in the past, separated by periods where you felt essentially back to your normal self, or is this the first time you've experienced this kind of stretch?

Oh, no, it's definitely not the first time. I really wish it was, because then maybe I could just chalk it up to a bad month or a passing phase, you know? Like maybe I just caught a bug or needed a vacation. But no, it’s happened before. It’s very much a cycle. 

I’ll have these stretches where I feel completely, wonderfully normal. I’ll be back to my old self, getting up early, organizing the house, repotting the ferns, actually calling people back and wanting to chat. I’ll think to myself, "Okay, thank goodness, that’s over, I’m finally out of the woods." The house feels bright again. But then... it just creeps back in. 

And I actually sat down with my planner not too long ago because I was trying to figure out when I last bought the special fertilizer for my orchids—I have to order it from this specific catalog, you see, because the store-bought stuff just burns the roots—and while I was flipping through the pages, I started noticing these huge, glaring gaps. Weeks and weeks where I hadn't written a single thing down. No notes, no reminders, nothing. And I started really looking back and doing the math. 

If you take all those stretches... the gray, guilty periods where I lose interest in things... they've added up to about seven months. Seven months! And I say "guilty" because that's a huge part of it for me, too. Along with the grayness, I just get this terrible, sinking guilt for absolutely no reason. I'll sit at that kitchen table feeling so incredibly guilty that I'm not doing anything, even though I don't even have a job to go to right now, but I just feel like a burden to the whole world. 

But yes, seven months. That’s more than half a year just gone, swallowed up by this fog. It’s honestly terrifying when you really stop and think about it, because you don’t realize how much time you’re losing when you’re actually in the middle of it. You just wake up and another day is gone, and then another week, and then you look back and realize you’ve spent all this time just staring at the wall or pushing food around your plate. I remember back in the fall, right around when the leaves were turning on the big oak tree we have out front, I thought I was finally turning a corner, I really did, but then by Thanksgiving I was right back under that heavy blanket again, just completely checked out...

During those depressive stretches, how much do these symptoms interfere with your ability to manage daily responsibilities, like household tasks or seeing friends and family—are you still able to keep up with most things, or do you find yourself unable to manage even basic day-to-day activities?

Well, it definitely gets in the way, and it’s so frustrating because, as I mentioned, I don't have a traditional nine-to-five job to go to right now, so you’d think I’d have all the time in the world to just manage my day. But it really does take a toll on the things I am trying to do. 

For instance, I’ve been doing this facilitator training—it’s a whole program I signed up for, and it requires a lot of reading and writing out modules—and I also run a private blog. It’s nothing huge, just a space for my own writing and networking, but I take it seriously. I usually sit at the desktop in the spare room, the one with the nice ergonomic chair my husband got me, and I try to work. But when I’m in one of those low stretches, I completely fall behind on both the training and the blog work. It’s like trying to wade through wet cement. I’ll sit there staring at the screen, and my projects and all the explanations I need to write out just become so incredibly hard to organize. I can’t seem to put step A before step B. I'll have three different drafts open, and I just can't string the thoughts together in a way that makes any sense, so I just end up abandoning it altogether. 

And of course, that spills over into the rest of the house. Because I'm falling behind and feeling so guilty and foggy about it, it creates this awful tension at home. My husband is a very routine-oriented person, bless his heart, and the tension has just made it so much harder to keep up our normal routines with him. We usually have this whole system, you know? We have our morning coffee together on the patio, we do our grocery shopping on Tuesday mornings, we have a set way we run the household. But when I can't even organize a simple paragraph for my blog, I certainly can't keep up with our daily schedule. The whole day just falls apart. And then the tension just sits there in the air between us, heavy and uncomfortable, because he doesn't know how to fix it, and I'm just too checked out to explain why I haven't done the things I said I was going to do. It just disrupts absolutely everything, from my personal projects right down to when we eat dinner.
During these depressive stretches, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—such as trouble falling asleep, waking up frequently, or waking up much earlier than you'd like?

You know, it’s funny you ask about sleep, because... well, my husband is a terribly light sleeper. I mean, if a neighbor's dog barks three streets over, he’s shifting around and adjusting his pillows, sighing heavily in the dark. We actually had to buy one of those white noise machines—the little dome ones where you twist the top to change the pitch of the fan sound? We keep it right on his side of the nightstand just so he can get some peace. 

But me? Even when I’m deep in one of those awful, heavy stretches where everything feels like wading through wet cement, my sleep itself doesn't really change at all. I don't lie awake staring at the ceiling for hours, and I definitely don't have that thing where you jolt awake at four in the morning and can't get back to sleep. 

I know I mentioned the midnight snacking in the kitchen earlier, but that’s not really because I’m tossing and turning and can't drift off. It’s more that I just... haven't gone to bed yet, or I'm just delaying the whole process of ending the day. But once I actually decide to go into the bedroom and pull the covers up—I have this wonderful heavy quilt I use, my grandmother actually made it—once my head hits the pillow, I'm out. I sleep straight through the night until the sun comes up. 

Honestly, it almost feels like my brain is just so incredibly exhausted from fighting through the fog and carrying around all that guilt all day that it just completely shuts down the second it gets the chance. I've heard of people who get so down that they can't sleep a single wink, and I always think how awful that must be, because that just isn't me. So, no, I haven't noticed any trouble falling asleep or waking up frequently. My sleep is probably the one thing that stays completely normal through all of it.
During those low, heavy stretches, have you ever had thoughts of not wanting to be alive, or thoughts of harming yourself?

Well... that's a hard question, but I want to be honest with you because I know it's important. You know I just told you about how well I sleep once I finally get under that heavy quilt my grandmother made? Well, sometimes, on the absolute worst nights... when that guilt I mentioned is just sitting on my chest like an absolute anvil, and the house is completely quiet except for that little white noise machine humming away on my husband's side of the bed... I'll lie there right before I drift off, and I'll catch myself thinking that it really would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up the next morning. 

If I could just stay asleep forever, just peacefully tucked in there, and not have to face the grayness or the tension in the house or the fact that I can't even write a simple blog post without my brain feeling like wet cement. It just feels like slipping away in my sleep would solve everything, you know? It would take the burden off my husband, and I wouldn't have to feel that awful, heavy sinking feeling anymore. It's almost like a fantasy of just... stopping. 

But—and I want to be very, very clear about this because I don't want you to worry that I'm going to do something drastic the second I leave your office—I haven't actually made a plan to hurt myself. I really haven't. I don't sit around thinking about how I would do it, or looking things up, or gathering things, or anything terrifying like that. It's more just this passive, exhausting wish that the universe would just pause and let me fade out while I'm already sleeping. Because actually taking steps to do something... well, first of all, that takes a kind of energy and organization that I absolutely do not have when I'm in that state, and second, I could never do that to my husband intentionally. Not with how much he already puts up with when my routines fall apart. So, no plans, no actual intent to harm myself... just those heavy thoughts on the really bad nights that not waking up at all might be a relief.

On days when you have these nighttime eating episodes, how is your appetite the next morning—do you find yourself skipping breakfast or having little interest in eating early in the day, regardless of whether you're in one of your low stretches or not?

Well, the mornings... you know, it’s funny you bring up the whole eating schedule, because honestly, that’s actually what finally pushed me to come in and see you. It wasn't just the mornings, it's that my eating has just been completely all over the place. I mean, absolutely chaotic. 

To answer your question, yes, if I've been up doing that midnight snacking, I have zero interest in breakfast when my husband and I sit down for our patio coffee. I'll just stare at my mug. But it’s not even just a morning thing, it’s the whole day, and it fluctuates so wildly. Some weeks, I barely touch dinner at all. My husband will make this lovely meal—he does this roasted chicken in a glass casserole dish we got for our anniversary, the one with the little painted handles—and I’ll just sit there pushing the food around my plate, completely devoid of an appetite. I feel terrible because he puts so much effort into keeping our routine going, but I just can't eat a proper meal. 

And then, it makes no sense, but other nights I’ll find myself just standing right there in the middle of the kitchen, in the pitch dark except for the little light from the range hood, just eating crackers and sweets after everyone’s gone to bed. I'll go right into the pantry—second shelf on the left, where we keep the saltines and these little lemon cookies I usually try to save for when we have company—and I just stand there eating them right out of the box while the house is dead quiet. 

So it's not just skipping breakfast, it's this whole bizarre pendulum swing. I go from barely touching a beautiful dinner to standing in the dark eating handfuls of crackers, and it just completely throws off our grocery shopping and our meal plans. It just got so incredibly out of hand and frustrating that I finally thought, 'Okay, I really need to make an appointment and talk to someone about this,' because I can't keep living on lemon cookies at midnight and black coffee in the morning.
Over the time you've been having these nighttime eating episodes, have you noticed any significant changes in your weight?

Weight... well, I honestly couldn't give you an exact number. We have this digital scale in the master bathroom—it's one of those sleek glass ones, tucked right under the edge of the vanity, and you have to tap it with your toe to wake it up before you step on—but I just haven't had the heart to use it lately. I kind of just sweep the bathmat over it so I don't have to look at it. 

But honestly, doctor, like I was just saying a moment ago, the exact number on the scale isn't even the main thing on my mind. It's the behavior itself. That's what really finally pushed me to come in and see you in the first place. It's just that my eating has been so completely all over the place that my body probably doesn't even know what to do with itself anymore. I mean, how could my weight possibly stabilize when, like I was telling you, some weeks I'll sit down and barely touch a single bite of dinner, and then other nights I'm standing right there in the pitch-black kitchen, eating handfuls of crackers and sweets long after my husband is fast asleep? 

It's just so chaotic. I suppose if I really think about it, my clothes—especially these old denim pants I wear when I'm out back tending to the hydrangeas—they do feel a bit different from week to week. Sometimes they're terribly loose and I need a belt, and other times they pinch right at the waist. But I just keep coming back to the fact that I can't keep living with this wild back-and-forth. Going from having absolutely zero appetite for a beautiful home-cooked meal to standing at the pantry shelves eating lemon cookies at midnight... it's just exhausting, and it makes me feel so out of control of my own body. So, I don't know my exact weight, but the way I'm eating is just a total mess.

Over the past few months, on average, how many nights per week does this pattern of skipping dinner and then eating crackers or sweets after everyone's asleep happen, and has it been happening this often for at least three months?

You know, my husband actually asked me something similar just the other day. He was looking at the grocery list, trying to figure out if we needed to buy more of those lemon cookies—which, by the way, I still feel absolutely terrible about eating, because they really are supposed to be saved for when his sister comes over for coffee on Sunday afternoons—but when he asked how often I was getting up and doing it, I realized I just couldn't give him a straight answer. 

And I can't really give you one either, doctor, as far as an exact number of nights per week or whether it's been exactly three months. I don't keep a calendar of it, and I'm not trying to be difficult, it's just... well, like I keep saying, and I know I'm repeating myself here, but it's really the main thing that finally pushed me to come in and get help: my eating has just been completely all over the place. There's just no rhyme or reason to it that I can track. 

I can't put a neat little timeline on it because there isn't a strict pattern. Some weeks I’ll go days where I barely touch dinner, just sitting there at the table while my husband eats, and then other nights, completely unpredictably, I’ll be standing right there in the dark kitchen eating crackers and sweets after everyone’s gone to bed. It’s not like every Tuesday and Thursday I do this, or like it started on a specific date. It’s just the sheer unpredictability of it all. It’s just this chaotic back-and-forth that never seems to settle into any kind of normal routine, and that's exactly why I'm sitting here talking to you today.

I... gosh, I honestly don't know. I really haven't noticed anything like that, to be perfectly frank with you. I wish I could give you a simple, straightforward answer, but my mind just kind of goes blank when I try to think about it. 

It’s like, with everything else being so completely upside down—the skipped dinners, the standing in the dark with the cracker box, the whole bizarre routine of it all—my brain just doesn't have the room to keep track of much else. I just haven't paid attention to it at all. My husband is usually the one who notices the little details, like when the mail hasn't been brought in or if I left the porch light on, but even he hasn't mentioned anything about that to me. 

So I really couldn't say. I just haven't noticed it happening, and I'd hate to just sit here and guess or make something up for you, because then we'd probably both just end up more confused. Everything has just been such a chaotic blur lately that I'm afraid I just don't have an answer for you on that one.

Thinking about your longest recent stretch of feeling completely back to normal mood-wise—say, several weeks in a row without any of that grayness—did the skipping-dinner-then-midnight-snacking pattern continue every day during that whole stretch, or did it let up significantly when your mood was good?

Normal mood-wise... gosh, you know, it's funny you ask that, because when I try to think about a stretch of time where I felt completely back to normal, without any of that heaviness or that gray feeling you mentioned, my mind just sort of swims. 

Let me think. I mean, maybe a few months ago? I remember we had this string of really beautiful, sunny days, and I spent almost every afternoon out in the yard, working on those hydrangeas I mentioned, and sweeping off the back deck. I felt pretty good then, relatively speaking. Lighter, you know? I was actually enjoying the fresh air instead of just staring out the window. But if you're asking me to match up how my mood was on those specific sunny weeks with whether or not I was skipping dinner and standing in the dark eating those lemon cookies... I just, I honestly can't piece it together for you. 

It’s like asking me to remember what socks I was wearing on a Tuesday three weeks ago. I want to say maybe the snacking let up? Because you'd think if I was feeling good, I'd sit down and eat a proper meal. My husband makes this wonderful roasted chicken with rosemary sometimes, and you'd think I would have sat there and eaten it with him if the grayness had lifted. But then again, maybe I still got up at midnight and went straight to the pantry anyway. 

The days and the nights, the good moods and the bad ones, they all just kind of bleed into one big chaotic mess in my memory lately. I really wish I had kept a journal or a log or something, because sitting here right now, trying to line up exactly how my mood was with what my eating habits were doing on those exact same days... I just draw a complete blank. I'm sorry, I know you're trying to find a pattern, but I just don't know if the eating thing continued every day or if it stopped when I felt better. I really couldn't tell you.

Aside from the guilt you feel about the depressive episodes in general, do you feel particularly upset, ashamed, or distressed specifically about the act of eating in the kitchen at night—even on nights when your mood is otherwise fine?

Well, you know, it's funny you mention the guilt, because that's something my husband and I were just talking about the other night when we were sitting on the couch watching that new mystery show on channel four. He asked me why I always look like I've been caught stealing from the collection plate when he walks into the kitchen in the morning and sees the empty cracker sleeves in the trash. And I tried to explain it to him, and I'll try to explain it to you, but it's just so hard to put into words. 

I mean, yes, obviously I feel terrible about the depressive episodes, the grayness, the way it makes me just completely useless around the house. But the kitchen thing... the standing in the dark eating those lemon cookies that are supposed to be for his sister, or the crackers, or whatever else I find... I honestly don't know if I feel specifically ashamed about the act of eating itself. 

It's more like... well, it's like I'm a ghost in my own house, you know? I'm standing there in the dark, and the refrigerator hums, and the floorboards creak, and I'm just chewing on these dry crackers, and I don't even really taste them half the time. It's just something to do with my hands, or my mouth, or I don't even know what. And on the nights when my mood is fine, if there even are nights when my mood is fine, which, like I said, is a whole other confusing topic... I just don't know if the feeling I have standing there is distress, exactly. 

It's more just a profound sense of... weirdness? Like, why am I doing this? Why can't I just eat a normal dinner at a normal time like a normal person? But is it shame? Am I upset specifically about the eating? I really couldn't say for sure. It all just gets mixed up in this big swirling pot of confusion and grayness and weird midnight habits, and trying to pull out one specific feeling about one specific part of it... I just don't think I can do it. I'm sorry, I know I'm probably not making much sense, but that's just honestly how it feels in my head right now.

Thinking back to before you ever had one of these depressive stretches for the very first time, had you already noticed this pattern of skipping dinner and then eating at night, or did it only start once the mood episodes began?

Well, see, that’s the thing, and actually, that’s a big part of why I finally made the appointment to come in and see you in the first place. I mean, my husband and I had been talking around it for a while, you know, just sort of dancing around the fact that things were getting strange, but what finally pushed me to pick up the phone and call the clinic was that my eating has just been completely all over the place. 

And to answer your question about when it started—before the grayness or after—I really have to think about that, because, like I said, it’s all just such a blur. But I do know that this whole pattern, this skipping dinner and then eating at night, it’s become such a defining part of whatever is going on with me right now. Some weeks, like I mentioned before, I’ll sit at the table with my husband, and he’ll have made that nice roasted chicken or a pork chop or something, and I just barely touch my dinner. I’ll push the peas around with my fork, maybe take a tiny bite of a roll, but I just have absolutely no interest in it. 

And then, sure enough, other nights, long after everyone’s gone to bed and the house is completely quiet, there I am. Standing in the dark in the kitchen, just eating crackers and sweets—those lemon cookies I told you about, or whatever else I can get my hands on. It’s like a completely different person takes over at 1:00 AM. 

So, did it start before the very first time I felt that heavy, depressive grayness? Gosh, I want to say... I want to say they sort of arrived together? Or maybe the eating thing started just a little bit before? It’s so hard to untangle it all now. But the fact that it’s gotten to this point, where my eating is just so erratic and strange—ignoring a perfectly good meal at 6:00 PM and then gorging on dry crackers in the dark at midnight—that was really the final straw that made me realize I couldn't just keep ignoring everything and hoping it would fix itself. I just knew I had to come in and talk to someone about it.

I'm honestly not sure. I really don't know how to answer that, to be perfectly honest with you. I haven't really noticed one way or the other. 

You have to understand, when things get into that heavy, gray area I was talking about, everything just sort of blurs together into this thick fog. So if you're asking me for specifics on that... I really couldn't say. I just don't know. My husband might know, because he's the one who pays attention to all the little details around the house—like when the car needs its oil changed, or when the dog needs his heartworm pill, or when my routine shifts even a tiny bit. He's very observant like that, bless his heart. He keeps the whole house running when I'm just sort of floating through it. 

But me? Sitting here right now, trying to think about it? I draw a complete blank. It’s like trying to read a book in a pitch-black room. I wish I could give you a clear-cut answer, I really do, because I know you're trying to put all these puzzle pieces together to figure out exactly what's going wrong with me, but I just don't have that piece to give you. I'm sorry to just ramble on about it without giving you anything useful, but I really just don't know.

Wait, I'm sorry, I just realized I completely lost track of what you just asked me. I was so caught up in trying to explain how my husband notices all these little things, and how the grayness just sort of swallows up my memory of everything else, that I think I completely talked right over your question. 

It’s terrible, I do this all the time lately. I’ll be in the middle of a thought, and it feels so important to get it all out, every little detail, because I want you to understand exactly what it’s like inside my head... but then I realize I’ve just been spinning my wheels and I haven't even answered what you wanted to know. 

Could you... could you please repeat what you just asked me? I promise I'll try to actually answer it this time, instead of just going on and on about the fog and my husband. I really do want to help you figure this out, I just get so tangled up in my own words sometimes. What was the question again?

Oh, right, right. Thank you for repeating it, I'm so sorry to make you say it all over again. You have the patience of a saint, you really do. But you know, even hearing it a second time, and really trying to sift through my memory to give you a proper answer... I honestly just don't know. 

It’s so frustrating, because I sit here and I want to be helpful, I want to hand you all the pieces to this puzzle neatly in a little box so we can figure it out together. But when I try to think about that, it’s just a blank space. I haven't really noticed anything like that one way or the other, or at least, if I did, it’s completely gone from my mind now. It’s exactly like when you walk into a room to get something and completely forget what you went in there for, except it’s like that for my own life right now. 

I really wish I could give you a clear 'yes' or 'no' on that, I truly do, but I'd just be making a complete guess at this point. And I certainly don't want to give you the wrong information and send us down the wrong path when you're trying so hard to help me get back on track. So, no, I just don't have an answer for that one, I'm afraid.

To be completely honest with you, I'm coming up empty on that one, too. I really haven't noticed anything like that at all. 

I know, I know, I'm probably sounding like a broken record today, just sitting here saying 'I don't know, I don't know' over and over again. It makes me feel like such a terrible patient. It's like I have no normal routine anymore. Some weeks, I'll sit down at the table with my husband, and I just barely touch my dinner. The thought of chewing and swallowing just feels so exhausting, like it’s too much effort. 

But then, on the flip side, there are other nights where I just can't seem to stop. It’s always late, after my husband has gone to bed and the house is completely quiet. I’ll be lying there, staring at the ceiling, and suddenly I just have to get up. I’ll go downstairs into the kitchen, and I just stand there in the dark, bathed in the light of the refrigerator, eating whatever I can get my hands on. It’s usually crackers, or those little sweets my husband keeps in the pantry, the ones with the powdered sugar on them. I’ll just stand there eating them, one after another, and I don't even really feel hungry, but I can't stop doing it. It’s like a compulsion. And then I wake up the next morning feeling so guilty and bloated, and I think, 'Why did I do that? Why couldn't I just stay in bed?'
